messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Vignette:
Mateo is a 24-year-old QA engineer who came to treatment months after surviving a man-made disaster that still feels unfinished to him. He had been on his commute when the incident happened, part of an ordinary morning that split cleanly into a before and after. He describes being in a crowded public space when chaos broke open around him: the sudden sound of impact and shattering, people screaming, bodies pushing in every direction, and the immediate conviction that someone had chosen to do this. What remains most vivid to him is not a single orderly memory but a series of jagged moments: turning and seeing strangers on the ground, hearing someone cry for help, and realizing he did not know where the danger was coming from or who might be responsible. In the middle of it, he remembers trying to move with others toward safety and at the same time registering people who were slower, stunned, or trapped in the crush. Since then, he has carried a fixed, painful belief that he should have protected other people and failed. He knows, when pressed, that he was one young man in a scene of mass panic, but that thought has never felt emotionally persuasive. What stays with him is the image of himself leaving while others were still behind him.

In the weeks after the disaster, Mateo found himself replaying alternate versions of that morning with relentless precision. On the train to work, in the shower, while trying to fall asleep, he would run through tiny changes as if one different decision could restore the world he had before. If he had left home five minutes earlier, if he had stood closer to one exit, if he had grabbed someone’s arm, if he had shouted louder. He thinks often about how life would have been different if the event had never occurred, and these thoughts have become woven into even neutral moments. A pleasant evening can suddenly turn into a comparison with the life he believes was taken from him. He has come to believe that nothing good can happen to him anymore, and he says this less dramatically than flatly, as though he is describing a rule he has learned.

Certain things now pierce straight through whatever composure he has managed. Conversation about crashes or accidents is especially difficult. At work, where quality assurance often involves bug triage meetings and postmortems, he has found that even routine discussion framed around what “went wrong,” “impact,” or “failure points” can hook him unexpectedly if a coworker shifts into talking about a real-world disaster in the news. During lunch breaks, when colleagues chat about a recent transit accident or a mass casualty story they saw online, he goes quiet, excuses himself, or stares at his screen until the room feels far away. One of the sensations that frightens him most is the beginning of detachment: the first unreal, floaty feeling that he is no longer fully in his body. When that starts, he becomes intensely alert to it, certain that if he lets it continue he will lose control completely. Related news has a similar effect. He stopped watching television and avoids films, documentaries, and articles about disasters because he cannot tolerate the first headline, the first clip of sirens or wreckage, the first panel of strangers explaining what happened.

His fear has generalized in a way that feels to him both logical and bleak. Because the original event was deliberately caused, Mateo is certain you can never know who will harm you. He studies faces in public and notices where people place their hands, how abruptly they move, whether they seem agitated. Police are especially difficult for him to be around. Their presence does not reassure him; it returns him instantly to the aftermath of that day, to barricades, commands, and the knowledge that something terrible has already happened. If he sees officers near the station or outside his office building, he changes course, waits inside a coffee shop, or orders a rideshare to avoid walking past them. These detours have made him late to work more than once and have narrowed his daily life without his intending it. Friends have stopped sending him links to news stories because he either ignores them or reacts sharply, and he has become more isolated than he was before.

By the time he sought help, Mateo was exhausted by how much effort ordinary life required. What finally brought him in was a recent incident in the office break room when coworkers began discussing a transportation disaster on the news. He felt the now-familiar wave of unreality, left abruptly, and spent the next hour in a restroom stall trying to steady himself while also thinking, with bitter certainty, that this was proof his life would never get better. He came to treatment frightened that the detached feeling will overtake him in public and that he will remain someone who failed others and can never trust anyone again. At the same time, he says quietly that he would like to believe there is still some future available to him, even if he cannot yet imagine what it looks like.
